title: Polar Coordinates and Conversions
subtitle: ClipSAT Printable Practice Suite (clipsat.org) • Topic 6.01 • 20 FRQs + 25 MCQs • Difficulty Progression • Cross-Lesson Synthesis

sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: Convert each polar point \((r, \theta)\) to rectangular coordinates (exact values):
Convert the polar point \(\left(4, 30^\circ\right)\) to Cartesian coordinates.
questions.answer: **Answer:** C. \(x=r\cos\theta=4\cos30^\circ=2\sqrt{3}\), \(y=r\sin\theta=4\sin30^\circ=2\).
questions.explanation: \(x=r\cos\theta=4\cos30^\circ=2\sqrt{3}\), \(y=r\sin\theta=4\sin30^\circ=2\).

questions.q: Convert the polar equation \(r = 6\cos\theta\) to rectangular form and identify the curve.
questions.answer: Multiply by \(r\): \(r^2 = 6r\cos\theta\), so \(x^2 + y^2 = 6x\), i.e. \((x - 3)^2 + y^2 = 9\): a circle with center \((3, 0)\) and radius 3.
questions.explanation: Multiply by \(r\): \(r^2 = 6r\cos\theta\), so \(x^2 + y^2 = 6x\), i.e. \((x - 3)^2 + y^2 = 9\): a circle with center \((3, 0)\) and radius 3.

questions.q: Convert each rectangular equation to polar form:
Convert the polar equation \(r = \frac{2}{1 - \sin\theta}\) to rectangular form.
questions.answer: \(r - r\sin\theta = 2\), so \(r = y + 2\). Squaring: \(x^2 + y^2 = (y + 2)^2 = y^2 + 4y + 4\), so \(x^2 = 4y + 4\) — a parabola.
questions.explanation: \(r - r\sin\theta = 2\), so \(r = y + 2\). Squaring: \(x^2 + y^2 = (y + 2)^2 = y^2 + 4y + 4\), so \(x^2 = 4y + 4\) — a parabola.

questions.q: Give two other pairs \((r,\theta)\) that represent the same point as \(\left(3, \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\): one with \(r>0\) and \(\theta\) outside \([0,2\pi)\), and one with \(r<0\).
questions.answer: Adding a full rotation: \(\left(3, \frac{\pi}{4}+2\pi\right) = \left(3,\frac{9\pi}{4}\right)\). Using negative \(r\) (add \(\pi\) to the angle): \(\left(-3, \frac{\pi}{4}+\pi\right) = \left(-3,\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)\).
questions.explanation: Adding a full rotation: \(\left(3, \frac{\pi}{4}+2\pi\right) = \left(3,\frac{9\pi}{4}\right)\). Using negative \(r\) (add \(\pi\) to the angle): \(\left(-3, \frac{\pi}{4}+\pi\right) = \left(-3,\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)\).

questions.q: Plot-reasoning: explain why the polar point \(\left(-2, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) corresponds to the same location as \(\left(2, \frac{3\pi}{2}\right)\).
questions.answer: A negative \(r\) means the point lies in the direction opposite to \(\theta\). Pointing at angle \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) (straight up) with \(r=-2\) places the point 2 units in the opposite direction, straight down — the same location as \(r=2\) at angle \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\) (also straight down).
questions.explanation: A negative \(r\) means the point lies in the direction opposite to \(\theta\). Pointing at angle \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) (straight up) with \(r=-2\) places the point 2 units in the opposite direction, straight down — the same location as \(r=2\) at angle \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\) (also straight down).

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: Convert \(\left(4,\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\) and \(\left(4,\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\) to rectangular coordinates, then find the distance between them, to two decimal places.
questions.answer: \(\left(4,\frac{\pi}{6}\right) \rightarrow (2\sqrt{3}, 2)\); \(\left(4,\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) \rightarrow (-2, 2\sqrt{3})\). Distance \(=\sqrt{(2\sqrt{3}+2)^2+(2-2\sqrt{3})^2} \approx \sqrt{29.86+2.14} = \sqrt{32} \approx 5.66\).
questions.explanation: \(\left(4,\frac{\pi}{6}\right) \rightarrow (2\sqrt{3}, 2)\); \(\left(4,\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) \rightarrow (-2, 2\sqrt{3})\). Distance \(=\sqrt{(2\sqrt{3}+2)^2+(2-2\sqrt{3})^2} \approx \sqrt{29.86+2.14} = \sqrt{32} \approx 5.66\).

questions.q: Convert the polar equation \(r^2 = 4\sin2\theta\) to note its symmetry, and identify it as a standard curve type.
questions.answer: This is a lemniscate (figure-eight curve). Rewriting \(r^2=4\sin2\theta = 8\sin\theta\cos\theta\), and using \(r^2=x^2+y^2\), \(r\cos\theta=x\), \(r\sin\theta=y\): multiplying both sides by \(r^2\) gives \((x^2+y^2)^2 = 8xy\).
questions.explanation: This is a lemniscate (figure-eight curve). Rewriting \(r^2=4\sin2\theta = 8\sin\theta\cos\theta\), and using \(r^2=x^2+y^2\), \(r\cos\theta=x\), \(r\sin\theta=y\): multiplying both sides by \(r^2\) gives \((x^2+y^2)^2 = 8xy\).

questions.q: Explain why, unlike rectangular coordinates, a single point can be represented by infinitely many polar coordinate pairs.
questions.target: Why polar coordinates are not unique
questions.answer: Adding any multiple of \(2\pi\) to \(\theta\) returns to the same direction, and reversing the sign of \(r\) while adding \(\pi\) to \(\theta\) also gives the same point — so every point has infinitely many valid \((r,\theta)\) representations, unlike the one-to-one rectangular system.
questions.explanation: Adding any multiple of \(2\pi\) to \(\theta\) returns to the same direction, and reversing the sign of \(r\) while adding \(\pi\) to \(\theta\) also gives the same point — so every point has infinitely many valid \((r,\theta)\) representations, unlike the one-to-one rectangular system.

questions.q: The pole (origin) is a special case in polar coordinates. Explain why.
questions.target: Why polar coordinates are not unique
questions.answer: The pole corresponds to \(r=0\) for ANY value of \(\theta\) — every angle gives the same point (the origin) when \(r=0\), so the pole has no single well-defined angle.
questions.explanation: The pole corresponds to \(r=0\) for ANY value of \(\theta\) — every angle gives the same point (the origin) when \(r=0\), so the pole has no single well-defined angle.

questions.q: Convert the rectangular equation \(x^2-y^2=4\) (a hyperbola) to polar form.
questions.answer: \(r^2\cos^2\theta-r^2\sin^2\theta=4 \Rightarrow r^2(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)=4 \Rightarrow r^2\cos(2\theta)=4\).
questions.explanation: \(r^2\cos^2\theta-r^2\sin^2\theta=4 \Rightarrow r^2(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)=4 \Rightarrow r^2\cos(2\theta)=4\).

questions.q: Convert the polar point \(\left(-4,\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\) (negative \(r\)) to rectangular coordinates.
questions.target: More point conversions with negative r
questions.answer: \(x=r\cos\theta=-4\cos\frac{\pi}{6}=-4\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=-2\sqrt{3}\). \(y=r\sin\theta=-4\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=-4\cdot\frac{1}{2}=-2\). Point: \((-2\sqrt{3},-2)\).
questions.explanation: \(x=r\cos\theta=-4\cos\frac{\pi}{6}=-4\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=-2\sqrt{3}\). \(y=r\sin\theta=-4\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=-4\cdot\frac{1}{2}=-2\). Point: \((-2\sqrt{3},-2)\).

questions.q: Convert the rectangular point \((-4,-4)\) to polar coordinates with \(r>0\) and \(0\leq\theta<2\pi\).
questions.target: More point conversions with negative r
questions.answer: \(r=\sqrt{16+16}=4\sqrt{2}\). Both coordinates negative places this in QIII, reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{4}\): \(\theta=\pi+\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{5\pi}{4}\).
questions.explanation: \(r=\sqrt{16+16}=4\sqrt{2}\). Both coordinates negative places this in QIII, reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{4}\): \(\theta=\pi+\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{5\pi}{4}\).

sections.heading: Part III — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (15–20)

questions.q: The Archimedean spiral \(r=\theta\) has no simple rectangular equivalent, but explain qualitatively why it spirals outward as \(\theta\) increases.
questions.answer: Since \(r=\theta\), the radius grows in direct proportion to the angle swept — each additional full rotation (\(2\pi\) radians) pushes \(r\) out by \(2\pi\) more units, producing evenly-spaced spiral arms rather than a closed curve.
questions.explanation: Since \(r=\theta\), the radius grows in direct proportion to the angle swept — each additional full rotation (\(2\pi\) radians) pushes \(r\) out by \(2\pi\) more units, producing evenly-spaced spiral arms rather than a closed curve.

questions.q: Convert the polar point \(\left(6, 45^\circ\right)\) to Cartesian coordinates.
questions.answer: **Answer:** B. \(x=r\cos\theta=6\cos45^\circ=3\sqrt{2}\), \(y=r\sin\theta=6\sin45^\circ=3\sqrt{2}\).
questions.explanation: \(x=r\cos\theta=6\cos45^\circ=3\sqrt{2}\), \(y=r\sin\theta=6\sin45^\circ=3\sqrt{2}\).

questions.q: A second aircraft is detected at rectangular coordinates \((30,-40)\) relative to the same radar station. Convert to polar coordinates \((r,\theta)\) with \(r>0\) and \(0\leq\theta<2\pi\), to two decimal places.
questions.cross_lesson: 2.03 Graphs of Sine and Cosine Functions
questions.answer: \(r=\sqrt{30^2+40^2}=\sqrt{900+1600}=\sqrt{2500}=50\) km. Reference angle \(=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{40}{30}\right)\approx53.13°\approx0.93\) rad. Since \(x>0,y<0\) (QIV): \(\theta\approx2\pi-0.93\approx5.35\) rad.
questions.explanation: \(r=\sqrt{30^2+40^2}=\sqrt{900+1600}=\sqrt{2500}=50\) km. Reference angle \(=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{40}{30}\right)\approx53.13°\approx0.93\) rad. Since \(x>0,y<0\) (QIV): \(\theta\approx2\pi-0.93\approx5.35\) rad.

questions.q: Convert the rectangular equation of a vertical line, \(x=5\), to polar form, and explain why the result is not simply a constant \(r\).
questions.cross_lesson: 2.04 Law of Sines and Law of Cosines
questions.answer: \(r\cos\theta=5 \Rightarrow r=\frac{5}{\cos\theta}=5\sec\theta\). Unlike a circle centered at the pole (constant \(r\)), a vertical line's distance from the pole varies with direction \(\theta\), so \(r\) must depend on \(\theta\) through the secant function.
questions.explanation: \(r\cos\theta=5 \Rightarrow r=\frac{5}{\cos\theta}=5\sec\theta\). Unlike a circle centered at the pole (constant \(r\)), a vertical line's distance from the pole varies with direction \(\theta\), so \(r\) must depend on \(\theta\) through the secant function.

questions.q: Convert the polar equation \(r=6\) to rectangular form, and explain in one sentence why this equation contains no \(\theta\) term.
questions.cross_lesson: 3.01 The Unit Circle and Exact Values
questions.answer: \(x^2+y^2=36\) (squaring both sides of \(r=6\)). There is no \(\theta\) term because every direction from the pole at distance \(6\) satisfies the equation equally — the curve is a full circle, independent of angle.
questions.explanation: \(x^2+y^2=36\) (squaring both sides of \(r=6\)). There is no \(\theta\) term because every direction from the pole at distance \(6\) satisfies the equation equally — the curve is a full circle, independent of angle.

questions.q: Level 2 · MediumFind all real solutions to the trigonometric equation \(2\cos^2\theta + 3\sin\theta - 3 = 0\) on the interval \([0, 2\pi)\).
questions.answer: Step 1 (Convert to Single Trig Ratio): Substitute \(\cos^2\theta = 1 - \sin^2\theta\): \(2(1 - \sin^2\theta) + 3\sin\theta - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow 2 - 2\sin^2\theta + 3\sin\theta - 3 = 0.\) \(-2\sin^2\theta + 3\sin\theta - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow 2\sin^2\theta - 3\sin\theta + 1 = 0.\) Step 2 (Factor the Quadratic in \(\sin\theta\)): \((2\sin\theta - 1)(\sin\theta - 1) = 0.\) Step 3 (Solve the Linear Factors):\(\sin\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\).\(2\sin\theta - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \frac{1}{2}\). In \([0, 2\pi)\), sine is positive in Quadrants I and II with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\): \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{6} \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \theta = \pi - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6}.\) The solution set is \(\left\{ \frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{5\pi}{6} \right\}\).
questions.explanation: Step 1 (Convert to Single Trig Ratio): Substitute \(\cos^2\theta = 1 - \sin^2\theta\): \(2(1 - \sin^2\theta) + 3\sin\theta - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow 2 - 2\sin^2\theta + 3\sin\theta - 3 = 0.\) \(-2\sin^2\theta + 3\sin\theta - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow 2\sin^2\theta - 3\sin\theta + 1 = 0.\) Step 2 (Factor the Quadratic in \(\sin\theta\)): \((2\sin\theta - 1)(\sin\theta - 1) = 0.\) Step 3 (Solve the Linear Factors):\(\sin\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\).\(2\sin\theta - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \frac{1}{2}\). In \([0, 2\pi)\), sine is positive in Quadrants I and II with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\): \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{6} \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \theta = \pi - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6}.\) The solution set is \(\left\{ \frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{5\pi}{6} \right\}\).

questions.q: Convert the polar point \(\left(8, 60^\circ\right)\) to Cartesian coordinates.
questions.answer: **Answer:** B. \(x=r\cos\theta=8\cos60^\circ=4\), \(y=r\sin\theta=8\sin60^\circ=4\sqrt{3}\).

questions.q: The function \(f\) is defined for all real numbers by \(f(x) = x^3 + 3x - 5.\) Between which pair of consecutive integers does the unique real root of the equation \(f(x) = 0\) lie?
questions.answer: To locate the root using the change of sign method, evaluate \(f(x)\) at consecutive integer values: \(f(0) = (0)^3 + 3(0) - 5 = -5 0\) Since \(f(x)\) is a continuous polynomial function and there is a sign change between \(x = 1\) (where \(f(1) 0\)), by the Intermediate Value Theorem, a root of \(f(x) = 0\) lies between \(1\) and \(2\). Checking the other intervals: - On \([0, 1]\), \(f(0) = -5\) and \(f(1) = -1\) (no sign change). - On \([2, 3]\), \(f(2) = 9\) and \(f(3) = 31\) (no sign change). - On \([-1, 0]\), \(f(-1) = -9\) and \(f(0) = -5\) (no sign change).
questions.explanation: To locate the root using the change of sign method, evaluate \(f(x)\) at consecutive integer values: \(f(0) = (0)^3 + 3(0) - 5 = -5 0\) Since \(f(x)\) is a continuous polynomial function and there is a sign change between \(x = 1\) (where \(f(1) 0\)), by the Intermediate Value Theorem, a root of \(f(x) = 0\) lies between \(1\) and \(2\). Checking the other intervals: - On \([0, 1]\), \(f(0) = -5\) and \(f(1) = -1\) (no sign change). - On \([2, 3]\), \(f(2) = 9\) and \(f(3) = 31\) (no sign change). - On \([-1, 0]\), \(f(-1) = -9\) and \(f(0) = -5\) (no sign change).

questions.q: The diagram shows the graph of the function \(y = f(x)\). The coordinates of the points A, B, and C are given. The graph is transformed by a translation of 3 units to the right and 2 units down. What are the new coordinates of point A?
questions.answer: The original coordinates of point A are (-4, 2). A translation of 3 units to the right means we add 3 to the x-coordinate. A translation of 2 units down means we subtract 2 from the y-coordinate. New x-coordinate = Original x-coordinate + 3 = -4 + 3 = -1 New y-coordinate = Original y-coordinate - 2 = 2 - 2 = 0 Therefore, the new coordinates of point A are (-1, 0).
questions.explanation: The original coordinates of point A are (-4, 2). A translation of 3 units to the right means we add 3 to the x-coordinate. A translation of 2 units down means we subtract 2 from the y-coordinate. New x-coordinate = Original x-coordinate + 3 = -4 + 3 = -1 New y-coordinate = Original y-coordinate - 2 = 2 - 2 = 0 Therefore, the new coordinates of point A are (-1, 0).

questions.q: Convert the polar point \(\left(2, 90^\circ\right)\) to Cartesian coordinates.
questions.answer: **Answer:** A. \(x=r\cos\theta=2\cos90^\circ=0\), \(y=r\sin\theta=2\sin90^\circ=2\).
questions.explanation: \(x=r\cos\theta=2\cos90^\circ=0\), \(y=r\sin\theta=2\sin90^\circ=2\).

questions.q: Convert the polar point \(\left(10, 120^\circ\right)\) to Cartesian coordinates.
questions.answer: **Answer:** A. \(x=r\cos\theta=10\cos120^\circ=-5\), \(y=r\sin\theta=10\sin120^\circ=5\sqrt{3}\).
questions.explanation: \(x=r\cos\theta=10\cos120^\circ=-5\), \(y=r\sin\theta=10\sin120^\circ=5\sqrt{3}\).

questions.q: The points A, B, and C have coordinates A(2, 5), B(k, 1), and C(8, -3). If A, B, and C are collinear, find the value of \(k\).
questions.target: Why polar coordinates are not unique
questions.answer: For three points A, B, and C to be collinear, the gradient of the line segment AB must be equal to the gradient of the line segment BC (or AC). The gradient formula between two points \((x_1, y_1)\) and \((x_2, y_2)\) is given by \(m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}\). Gradient of AB, \(m_{AB} = \frac{1 - 5}{k - 2} = \frac{-4}{k - 2}\). Gradient of BC, \(m_{BC} = \frac{-3 - 1}{8 - k} = \frac{-4}{8 - k}\). Equating the gradients: \(\frac{-4}{k - 2} = \frac{-4}{8 - k}\) Since the numerators are equal and non-zero, the denominators must be equal: \(k - 2 = 8 - k\) Add \(k\) to both sides: \(2k - 2 = 8\) Add 2 to both sides: \(2k = 10\) Divide by 2: \(k = 5\) Common algebraic trap: A student might incorrectly assume that \(k-2 = -(8-k)\) leading to \(k-2 = -8+k\) which has no solution. Alternatively, cross-multiplying and making an error in expansion is also a pitfall.
questions.explanation: For three points A, B, and C to be collinear, the gradient of the line segment AB must be equal to the gradient of the line segment BC (or AC). The gradient formula between two points \((x_1, y_1)\) and \((x_2, y_2)\) is given by \(m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}\). Gradient of AB, \(m_{AB} = \frac{1 - 5}{k - 2} = \frac{-4}{k - 2}\). Gradient of BC, \(m_{BC} = \frac{-3 - 1}{8 - k} = \frac{-4}{8 - k}\). Equating the gradients: \(\frac{-4}{k - 2} = \frac{-4}{8 - k}\) Since the numerators are equal and non-zero, the denominators must be equal: \(k - 2 = 8 - k\) Add \(k\) to both sides: \(2k - 2 = 8\) Add 2 to both sides: \(2k = 10\) Divide by 2: \(k = 5\) Common algebraic trap: A student might incorrectly assume that \(k-2 = -(8-k)\) leading to \(k-2 = -8+k\) which has no solution. Alternatively, cross-multiplying and making an error in expansion is also a pitfall.

sections.heading: Part V — Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQs): Intermediate Exam Application (29–37)

questions.q: Consider the quadratic equation \(2x^2 - (k - 1)x + (k + 1) = 0\) where \(k\) is a real constant. The equation has two non-real complex conjugate roots. If the imaginary parts of the roots have a magnitude of \(\frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\), what is the greatest possible value of \(k\)?
questions.answer: To find the parameter \(k\), apply the quadratic formula to \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\): \(x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\) Identify the coefficients from the given equation: \(a = 2, \quad b = -(k - 1), \quad c = k + 1\) Compute the discriminant \(\Delta\): \(\Delta = [-(k - 1)]^2 - 4(2)(k + 1) = (k^2 - 2k + 1) - (8k + 8) = k^2 - 10k - 7\) Since the equation has non-real complex roots, \(\Delta 0\), confirming the roots are non-real. The greatest possible value of \(k\) is \(7\). - Misconception 3 arises from selecting the smaller valid parameter value. - Misconception 10 arises from using \(2\) instead of \(2a = 4\) in the denominator of the quadratic formula, leading to \(-k^2 + 10k + 7 = 7 \Rightarrow k = 10\). - Misconception 5 arises from taking the midpoint/axis of symmetry of the two values of \(k\).
questions.explanation: To find the parameter \(k\), apply the quadratic formula to \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\): \(x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\) Identify the coefficients from the given equation: \(a = 2, \quad b = -(k - 1), \quad c = k + 1\) Compute the discriminant \(\Delta\): \(\Delta = [-(k - 1)]^2 - 4(2)(k + 1) = (k^2 - 2k + 1) - (8k + 8) = k^2 - 10k - 7\) Since the equation has non-real complex roots, \(\Delta 0\), confirming the roots are non-real. The greatest possible value of \(k\) is \(7\). - Misconception 3 arises from selecting the smaller valid parameter value. - Misconception 10 arises from using \(2\) instead of \(2a = 4\) in the denominator of the quadratic formula, leading to \(-k^2 + 10k + 7 = 7 \Rightarrow k = 10\). - Misconception 5 arises from taking the midpoint/axis of symmetry of the two values of \(k\).

questions.q: What are the solutions to the quadratic equation \(x^2 - 6x + 13 = 0\)?
questions.answer: To solve the quadratic equation \(x^2 - 6x + 13 = 0\), use the quadratic formula \(x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\) with \(a = 1\), \(b = -6\), and \(c = 13\): \(x = \frac{-(-6) \pm \sqrt{(-6)^2 - 4(1)(13)}}{2(1)} = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 52}}{2} = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{-16}}{2}\) Since \(\sqrt{-16} = 4i\), simplify the expression: \(x = \frac{6 \pm 4i}{2} = 3 \pm 2i\) - \(x = 3 \pm 4i\) occurs if the radical term is not divided by the denominator \(2\). - \(x = -3 \pm 2i\) occurs from a sign error when computing \(-b\). - \(x = 3 \pm 2\) occurs from ignoring the imaginary unit \(i\) and treating \(\sqrt{-16}\) as \(4\).
questions.explanation: To solve the quadratic equation \(x^2 - 6x + 13 = 0\), use the quadratic formula \(x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\) with \(a = 1\), \(b = -6\), and \(c = 13\): \(x = \frac{-(-6) \pm \sqrt{(-6)^2 - 4(1)(13)}}{2(1)} = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 52}}{2} = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{-16}}{2}\) Since \(\sqrt{-16} = 4i\), simplify the expression: \(x = \frac{6 \pm 4i}{2} = 3 \pm 2i\) - \(x = 3 \pm 4i\) occurs if the radical term is not divided by the denominator \(2\). - \(x = -3 \pm 2i\) occurs from a sign error when computing \(-b\). - \(x = 3 \pm 2\) occurs from ignoring the imaginary unit \(i\) and treating \(\sqrt{-16}\) as \(4\).

questions.q: Consider the quadratic equation \(x^2 - 8x + 15 = 0\). What are the roots of this equation?
questions.answer: To find the roots of the quadratic equation \(x^2 - 8x + 15 = 0\), we can factor the quadratic expression. We are looking for two numbers that multiply to 15 and add up to -8. These numbers are -3 and -5. Therefore, the factored form of the equation is \((x-3)(x-5) = 0\). Setting each factor to zero, we get \(x-3=0\) which gives \(x=3\), and \(x-5=0\) which gives \(x=5\). Thus, the roots are \(x=3\) and \(x=5\).
questions.explanation: To find the roots of the quadratic equation \(x^2 - 8x + 15 = 0\), we can factor the quadratic expression. We are looking for two numbers that multiply to 15 and add up to -8. These numbers are -3 and -5. Therefore, the factored form of the equation is \((x-3)(x-5) = 0\). Setting each factor to zero, we get \(x-3=0\) which gives \(x=3\), and \(x-5=0\) which gives \(x=5\). Thus, the roots are \(x=3\) and \(x=5\).

questions.q: Which is NOT a quadratic equation?
questions.answer: Applying Quadratics & Complex Numbers principles, Cubic, not quadratic. Therefore, the verified correct option is \(x^3+2x=0\).
questions.explanation: Applying Quadratics & Complex Numbers principles, Cubic, not quadratic. Therefore, the verified correct option is \(x^3+2x=0\).

questions.q: An ellipse has equation \(\frac{x^2}{36} + \frac{y^2}{20} = 1\). What are the coordinates of its foci?

questions.q: The graph of the exponential function \(f(x) = a \cdot b^x + c\) is shown in the \(xy\)-plane, where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are constants with \(b > 0\) and \(b eq 1\). The function has a horizontal asymptote at \(y = -4\) and passes through the points \((0, -1)\) and \((2, 8)\). What is the value of \(f(-1)\)?
questions.answer: To determine \(f(-1)\), we first find the constants \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\): 1. **Horizontal Asymptote:** For an exponential function of the form \(f(x) = a \cdot b^x + c\), as the exponential term approaches zero, the function approaches its horizontal asymptote \(y = c\). Given that the asymptote is \(y = -4\), we have: \(c = -4\) 2. **Use the Point \((0, -1)\):** Substitute \(x = 0\) and \(f(0) = -1\): \(f(0) = a \cdot b^0 - 4 = -1\) \(a(1) - 4 = -1 \Rightarrow a = 3\) 3. **Use the Point \((2, 8)\):** Substitute \(x = 2\) and \(f(2) = 8\): \(f(2) = 3 \cdot b^2 - 4 = 8\) \(3b^2 = 12 \Rightarrow b^2 = 4\) Since the base of an exponential function must be positive (\(b > 0\)), \(b = 2\). Thus, the function is \(f(x) = 3 \cdot 2^x - 4\). 4. **Evaluate \(f(-1)\):** \(f(-1) = 3 \cdot 2^{-1} - 4 = 3 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) - 4 = \frac{3}{2} - \frac{8}{2} = -\frac{5}{2}\) Common algebraic traps include: - Forgetting the horizontal shift parameter \(c\), leading to impossible base equations. - Confusing negative exponents, such as evaluating \(2^{-1}\) as \(-2\) instead of \(\frac{1}{2}\). - Neglecting the asymptote subtraction when calculating \(f(-1)\), yielding \(\frac{3}{2}\).

questions.q: Determine the complete set of real values of the constant \(k\) for which the equation \(2\cos 2\theta - 4\sin\theta = k\) has at least one real solution for \(\theta\).
questions.answer: To find the set of values of \(k\) for which real solutions exist, we express the left-hand side entirely in terms of \(\sin\theta\). Using the double-angle identity \(\cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta\): \(2(1 - 2\sin^2\theta) - 4\sin\theta = k\) \(-4\sin^2\theta - 4\sin\theta + 2 = k\) Let \(u = \sin\theta\). Since \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\), \(u\) is constrained to the closed interval \([-1, 1]\). The problem reduces to finding the range of the quadratic function \(f(u) = -4u^2 - 4u + 2, \quad u \in [-1, 1].\) 1. **Find the vertex (stationary point):** \(u_v = -\frac{b}{2a} = -\frac{-4}{2(-4)} = -\frac{1}{2}\) Since \(-\frac{1}{2} \in [-1, 1]\), this critical point lies within the domain. The value of \(f\) at the vertex is: \(f\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = -4\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 - 4\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) + 2 = -4\left(\frac{1}{4}\right) + 2 + 2 = 3\) Since the leading coefficient is negative (\(-4 < 0\)), the parabola opens downwards, making \(3\) the maximum value. 2. **Evaluate at the domain endpoints:** \(f(-1) = -4(-1)^2 - 4(-1) + 2 = -4 + 4 + 2 = 2\) \(f(1) = -4(1)^2 - 4(1) + 2 = -4 - 4 + 2 = -6\) 3. **Determine the range:** The absolute minimum on \([-1, 1]\) is \(\min(3, 2, -6) = -6\), and the absolute maximum is \(3\). Since \(f(u)\) is continuous on \([-1, 1]\), the range of \(f(u)\) is \([-6, 3]\). Hence, the equation has real solutions if and only if \(-6 \leq k \leq 3\). **Common Traps:** - Setting the discriminant \(\Delta \geq 0\) yields \(k \leq 3\), but overlooks the restriction \(|u| \leq 1\), incorrectly extending the lower bound to \(-\infty\). - Evaluating only at the domain endpoints \(u = \pm 1\) yields \([-6, 2]\), missing the maximum occurring at the vertex \(u = -\frac{1}{2}\). - Using the incorrect identity \(\cos 2\theta = 2\sin^2\theta - 1\) leads to \([-3, 6]\).

questions.q: Find the set of all real solutions to the equation \(\log_2(x - 1) - \log_4(x + 14) = 1\)
questions.answer: To solve the equation, we first express all logarithms in the same base using the change of base formula: \(\log_4(x + 14) = \frac{\log_2(x + 14)}{\log_2 4} = \frac{\log_2(x + 14)}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\log_2(x + 14)\) Substitute this back into the original equation: \(\log_2(x - 1) - \frac{1}{2}\log_2(x + 14) = 1\) Multiply through by \(2\): \(2\log_2(x - 1) - \log_2(x + 14) = 2\) Apply the power law and the quotient law of logarithms: \(\log_2\left((x - 1)^2\right) - \log_2(x + 14) = 2 \Rightarrow \log_2\left(\frac{(x - 1)^2}{x + 14}\right) = 2\) Convert from logarithmic form to exponential form: \(\frac{(x - 1)^2}{x + 14} = 2^2 = 4\) Clear the denominator and expand: \((x - 1)^2 = 4(x + 14)\) \(x^2 - 2x + 1 = 4x + 56\) \(x^2 - 6x - 55 = 0\) Factor the quadratic equation: \((x - 11)(x + 5) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 11 \quad \mathrm{or} \quad x = -5\) Now, we must consider the domain of the original logarithmic expressions: - For \(\log_2(x - 1)\) to be defined, \(x - 1 > 0 \Rightarrow x > 1\). - For \(\log_4(x + 14)\) to be defined, \(x + 14 > 0 \Rightarrow x > -14\). Thus, the domain requires \(x > 1\). - For \(x = -5\), the term \(\log_2(-5 - 1) = \log_2(-6)\) is undefined in the real numbers. Hence, \(x = -5\) is an extraneous solution introduced by squaring. - For \(x = 11\), \(\log_2(10) - \log_4(25) = \log_2(10) - \log_2(5) = \log_2(2) = 1\), which is valid. Therefore, the only real solution is \(x = 11\). Misconception Traps: - Choice B includes the extraneous root \(x = -5\), failing to verify the domain requirement \(x > 1\). - Choice C arises from an incorrect factorization of the quadratic (e.g., confusing signs as \((x + 11)(x - 5) = 0\)). - Choice D arises from failing to change the base of \(\log_4\) and solving \(\frac{x + 14}{x - 1} = 2\).

questions.q: The rational function \(f\) is defined for all real \(x otin \{-1, 2\}\) by \(f(x) = \frac{x^3 + kx + 7}{(x+1)(x-2)^2}\) where \(k\) is a constant. The partial fraction decomposition of \(f(x)\) takes the form \(A + \frac{B}{x+1} + \frac{C}{x-2} + \frac{D}{(x-2)^2}\) where \(A, B, C,\) and \(D\) are real constants. Given that \(C = 2\), find the value of \(k\).
questions.answer: Step 1: Determine the polynomial quotient \(A\). The degree of the numerator is \(3\) and the degree of the denominator is $1 + 2 = 3\(. Expanding the denominator gives: \)(x+1)(x-2)^2 = (x+1)(x^2 - 4x + 4) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 4\( Since the leading coefficient of both the numerator and the denominator is \)1\(, polynomial division yields a constant quotient: \)A = \frac{1}{1} = 1\( Step 2: Set up the algebraic identity. Multiplying both sides of the partial fraction expansion by \)(x+1)(x-2)^2\(: \)x^3 + kx + 7 \equiv A(x+1)(x-2)^2 + B(x-2)^2 + C(x+1)(x-2) + D(x+1)\( Step 3: Relate \)B\( and \)C\( by comparing coefficients of \)x^2\(. On the left-hand side, the coefficient of \)x^2\( is \)0\(. On the right-hand side, collecting the \)x^2\( terms: - \)A(x+1)(x-2)^2 = A(x^3 - 3x^2 + 4) \Rightarrow -3A\( - \)B(x-2)^2 = B(x^2 - 4x + 4) \Rightarrow +B\( - \)C(x+1)(x-2) = C(x^2 - x - 2) \Rightarrow +C\( - \)D(x+1) \Rightarrow 0\( Therefore: \)0 = -3A + B + C\( Substitute \)A = 1\( and the given value \)C = 2\(: \)-3(1) + B + 2 = 0 \Rightarrow B = 1\( Step 4: Solve for \)k\( by substituting \)x = -1\(. Setting \)x = -1\( eliminates the terms containing \)(x+1)\(: \)(-1)^3 + k(-1) + 7 = B(-1 - 2)^2\( \)-1 - k + 7 = B(-3)^2\( \)6 - k = 9B\( Since \)B = 1\(: \)6 - k = 9 \Rightarrow k = -3\( Common Algebraic Traps: - \)k = 24\(: Omits the quotient \)A\( (treating an improper fraction as proper), giving \)B + C = 0 \Rightarrow B = -2\(, leading to \)6 - k = -18 \Rightarrow k = 24\(. - \)k = 1\(: Substitutes \)x = 1\( instead of the root \)x = -1\(, obtaining \)1 + k + 7 = 9 \Rightarrow k = 1\(. - \)k = 3\(: Makes a sign error when rearranging \)6 - k = 9$.
